analysis.investment_thesis: KNR Constructions is a fast-growing infrastructure EPC play with a staggering PEG of ~0.23 (P/E 6.41 ÷ 27.6% earnings CAGR) — the kind of mispricing I'd drive a truck through. India's roads/highways capex supercycle is a tailwind you can see with your own eyes, and this company has quietly compounded earnings at 27.6% for nine straight years while trading below book value.
key_strengths: Exceptional PEG of 0.23 — P/E of 6.41 against a 9-year earnings CAGR of 27.6% is the definition of growth at a bargain price
Superior capital efficiency: ROE 27.2% and ROCE 28.6% — this company earns nearly 30 cents on every rupee of capital employed
Margin expansion story is intact — operating income grew at 28.2% CAGR vs revenue at 16.6%, showing structural profitability improvement
key_risks: Cash flow quality is alarming: OCF was positive in only 1 of the last 5 years (FY23: +₹1,194 Cr; FY25: -₹567 Cr) — profits on paper don't pay bills
Borrowings nearly tripled in two years (₹652 Cr in FY23 → ₹2,321 Cr in FY25), a debt surge that raises balance sheet fragility if project execution slips
Construction/EPC is inherently cyclical and government-dependent — order books can dry up fast if NHAI spending slows or elections cause policy delays
red_flags: Free cash flow deeply negative three consecutive years: FY22 -₹690 Cr, FY24 -₹374 Cr, FY25 -₹592 Cr — the HAM model is consuming cash faster than it reports profits
FY25 EBITDA jump to ₹1,913 Cr (from ₹1,192 Cr in FY24) with revenue up only 7% looks suspicious — margin expansion from 27% to 40%+ in one year warrants scrutiny before trusting the earnings number
analysis.detailed_analysis:
KNR Constructions is one of those stocks where the numbers almost seem too good to be true — and partly they are. The nine-year track record is genuinely impressive: revenue 16.6% CAGR, net profit 27.6% CAGR, and ROE consistently above 25%. At a P/E of 6.41 and P/B of 0.73, you're buying a high-ROCE business below book value. The PEG of 0.23 is in "ten-bagger candidate" territory on paper, and India's infrastructure push — something any observer can confirm by watching highway construction everywhere — is a multi-decade tailwind. The promoter holding of 48.81% alongside 19% DII backing signals alignment and institutional conviction.

The critical caveat Lynch must flag: this company doesn't actually generate cash consistently. The HAM (Hybrid Annuity Model) structure requires KNR to fund 40% of project costs upfront, creating persistent negative OCF and explaining the borrowings spike to ₹2,321 Cr. Lynch loves simple businesses you can understand — this one requires trusting that HAM annuities eventually monetize into real cash returns. The FY25 EBITDA anomaly (margins jumping 13 percentage points in one year) needs a clear explanation before full conviction. Score it a 7: the valuation and growth history are compelling enough to own a position, but the cash flow reality demands close quarterly monitoring.
